prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
On the evening of April 13, 1970, some 200,000 miles from Earth, the crew of Apollo 13 were finishing a routine television broadcast when a sudden bang shook their spacecraft. Commander Jim Lovell, command module pilot Jack Swigert and lunar module pilot Fred Haise had launched two days earlier on what was meant to be NASA's third landing on the Moon. Their target was the Fra Mauro highlands, a hilly region that geologists were eager to sample. The flight had gone so smoothly that the networks had declined to carry the crew's last television show, and the men had signed off to an audience that was mostly asleep or indifferent.

The bang came about fifty-five hours into the mission, when Mission Control asked the crew to stir the cryogenic tanks aboard the service module. This was a standard procedure meant to keep the supercooled oxygen and hydrogen from stratifying. Swigert flipped the switch, and a short time later Lovell and his crewmates heard a loud noise and felt the spacecraft shudder. Swigert reported the now famous understatement that they had a problem, and Lovell repeated it for the benefit of the controllers in Houston. Warning lights lit across the instrument panel, voltages dropped on the main electrical buses, and the crew soon saw through a window that the spacecraft was venting something into space.

The cause lay in a chain of small errors that had begun years earlier. Oxygen tank number two had been dropped slightly during handling at the factory, which damaged an internal fitting. During a ground test before launch, technicians had struggled to drain the tank, and they used heaters to boil off the oxygen. Those heaters had been designed for a lower voltage than the ground power supply delivered, and the high current fused the thermostat switches shut and burned away much of the wire insulation inside the tank. No one noticed. When Swigert turned on the stirring fans in flight, a spark from the bare wires ignited the oxygen and the tank ruptured, blowing off a panel of the service module and crippling the neighboring tank as well.

Within minutes it was clear that the command module, Odyssey, was dying. Its fuel cells needed oxygen to make electricity and water, and the oxygen was draining away into space. Flight director Gene Kranz and his team in Houston concluded that the crew would have to abandon the idea of landing on the Moon and that the priority was now simply to get the men home alive. The only other habitable vessel was the lunar module, Aquarius, a fragile craft built to support two men for about two days on the lunar surface. Controllers decided to use it as a lifeboat, and the crew moved into it while they shut down Odyssey to save its precious batteries for the final descent through the atmosphere.

The next problem was one of trajectory. Apollo 13 had been on a path that would have let it swing around the Moon and return to Earth, but it had since been moved onto a course that would have missed the planet altogether if left alone. Mission planners had to decide whether to fire the lunar module's descent engine immediately to turn the ship around, or to continue around the Moon first. They chose the second path, and about five hours after the explosion the crew used the descent engine to speed up their return. After passing behind the Moon, which put them farther from Earth than any humans had ever been, they fired the engine again to shorten the trip further.

The days that followed were a test of endurance. To conserve power, the crew switched off almost everything in the lunar module, including most of the heating. The cabin temperature fell to near freezing, water condensed on the walls, and the men slept very little. They also rationed water severely, with each man drinking only a few ounces a day, and Haise developed a kidney infection as a result. Meanwhile a more urgent threat emerged, which was carbon dioxide. The lunar module's lithium hydroxide canisters, which scrub exhaled gas from the air, were designed for two men over a short stay, and with three men aboard for four days they were saturating fast. The command module had spare canisters, but they were square and the lunar module's receptacles were round.

Engineers on the ground met the challenge with the materials that the crew had on board. Working in a room in Houston, they gathered a pile of items matching what was aboard, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, suit hoses and duct tape. Within hours they had devised a way to attach the square canister to the round opening, and they read the instructions to the crew step by step. Lovell, Swigert and Haise built the improvised adapter and watched as the carbon dioxide readings fell back to safe levels. It was one of the moments that most clearly showed how closely the people in space and on the ground were working together.

Another difficulty came when the crew had to correct their course by hand. A final burn was needed to keep the ship aligned with the narrow corridor through which it had to enter the atmosphere. Normally the guidance computer would have handled such a task, but the lunar module's systems were off and the usual alignment using stars was difficult because debris from the explosion glittered around the ship. Lovell used the Earth itself as a reference, holding its terminator in the window while Haise and Swigert timed the burn. It worked well enough that the spacecraft was set up properly for reentry.

Meanwhile the controllers faced the problem of bringing Odyssey back to life after days of cold soak. They had never planned for the command module to be powered down and then restarted in flight, and a team led by astronaut Charles Duke and others wrote a new checklist from scratch, testing it in simulators. As the spacecraft neared home, the crew first jettisoned the damaged service module and, for the first time, saw how severe the damage was. A whole side panel was missing, and the engine bell hung out at an odd angle. Lovell reported the sight to Houston, which at last understood how close the crew had come to losing everything.

Finally the crew moved back into Odyssey and released Aquarius, which had saved their lives, shortly before reentry. Their trip through the atmosphere meant a communications blackout that normally lasts about three minutes, and this time it stretched longer, as the people in Mission Control waited nervously with no word. Then, at a little after one in the afternoon Houston time on April 17, Swigert's voice came through, and the parachutes of Odyssey were seen drifting down toward the South Pacific near Samoa. The capsule splashed down within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima, and the crew emerged tired, thin and bearded but healthy.

Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, yet it became known as a successful failure. The investigation that followed, led by Edgar Cortright, traced the accident to the damaged tank and its faulty heaters, and NASA redesigned the oxygen system before the next flight. More lastingly, the episode showed what trained people could do under extraordinary pressure when they refused to give up. Lovell later said that the mission had taught him how much people could achieve when forced to, and for many who watched from the ground, the safe return of three men from the far side of the Moon was the greatest achievement of the entire Apollo program.
